source.title: What Features in Prompts Jailbreak LLMs? Investigating the Mechanisms Behind Attacks
source.authors: N. Kirch; Constantin Weisser; Severin Field; H. Yannakoudakis; Stephen T. Casper

record.file_problem: none; the provided text is the full paper, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports experiments on prompt-side features associated with jailbreak success, but does not test the refusal direction or any claim version’s specified mechanism. It discusses prior work on refusal directions.
record.gate_note: The study reports compliance changes from probe-guided latent perturbations, but these interventions target features predictive of jailbreak success, not the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction. It also reports probe classification and transfer results; those concern jailbreak-feature prediction rather than the refusal-direction claim.
record.test_reason: The study trains linear, MLP and transformer probes to predict jailbreak success from prompt activations, then perturbs activations along probe gradients. It never computes the harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction, ablates or adds it, or measures whether jailbreaks suppress it. Arditi et al. is cited only as related work and as an example of linear steering. The authors argue jailbreak features are non-universal and non-linear, which touches V3's framing, but they measure nothing about the refusal direction itself. The results therefore fit no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. To add: the authors frame the results as challenging the assumption that jailbreak-related features are universal or easily isolated by linear methods, citing Arditi et al. among others. They also claim defensive MLP perturbations match or beat supervised safety fine-tuning without degrading MMLU.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains probes to predict jailbreak success from prompt representations and applies gradient-guided latent perturbations. It does not use harmful-minus-harmless mean activations, ablate a refusal direction, or add that direction.
record.method_sensitivity: Probe architecture affects intervention strength, with MLP-guided interventions reported as most effective; intervention depth also changes compliance outcomes in the early, middle, and late layer experiments. MMLU-based filtering determines which configurations are retained for the main results.

fits_no_version.finding: Probe-guided latent perturbations shift harmful compliance: MLP offensive about 41% and MLP defensive about 4.8%, versus 21% with no intervention, averaged over five models at the middle layer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prompt-side features predictive of jailbreak success can be causally steered to raise or lower harmful compliance, with non-linear probes more effective than linear ones.

fits_no_version.finding: Probes trained on all but one attack type often perform near or below chance on the held-out attack (mean held-out accuracy about 0.41–0.79 by model and probe; Figure 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Features predicting jailbreak success are attack-family-specific rather than one universal direction.

fits_no_version.finding: Intervention settings were kept only if MMLU stayed near baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Probe-guided jailbreak-feature interventions can be tuned to preserve MMLU.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 8th BlackboxNLP Workshop: Analyzing and Interpreting Neural Networks for NLP
record.problems: The experiments concern jailbreak-success features rather than the claimed refusal direction. The main compliance configurations are selected using MMLU performance, and the reported compliance outcomes rely on the HarmBench autograder. The text does not provide a direct test of the claim’s direction ablation or harmless-request refusal induction.
record.rows_left_out: Probe accuracies and cross-layer or held-out-attack transfer results in Sections 4.1–4.3 and Figures 3–5 were not recorded because they measure jailbreak-success classification, not the claim’s refusal direction or the behavior specified by a claim version. Additional intervention-depth and single-layer results in Appendices H and I were not extracted; they likewise concern probe-guided jailbreak-feature perturbations, and the flattened plots do not reliably provide method-to-value assignments.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction, no ablation or addition, no harmless-refusal induction.
Does not measure whether jailbreaks suppress the refusal direction, and no training against its ablation.
Refusal geometry is not characterised; only jailbreak-success probes are studied.
Harmfulness and refusal representations are not separated.
No transfer of the refusal direction across languages, variants, or base and instruct models.
Refusal training is not varied. Ministral, which lacks safety tuning, is only noted in passing.

record.verdict_notes: Figure 6 values were mapped by assuming descending bar order. The constant control (21.0) and fine-tune (11.8) values across the Figure 14 early, middle and late panels support the mapping, but researchers should verify it against the figure. The paper's anti-universality argument concerns jailbreak-success probes and does not test the refusal direction, so it is not counted as T5 on V3.

versions.untested_parts: Does not find or ablate the difference-in-means refusal direction, induce refusals to harmless requests, or assess other abilities for that direction.
Does not test whether jailbreaks suppress the refusal direction or train against its ablation.
Does not characterize the geometry or number of refusal directions.
Does not separate harmfulness judgments from refusal decisions.
Does not test transfer of the refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models.
Does not vary refusal training or test when refusal is trained.

rows.operation_detail: Gradient-guided perturbation using an MLP probe trained to distinguish successful from unsuccessful jailbreak prompts; perturbations applied at a selected middle layer.
rows.baseline: Unperturbed baseline; numeric value not stated in text
rows.value: Higher attack success rates than linear perturbations and the unperturbed baseline; numerical value not stated in text
rows.note: Aggregate result across five models. The plotted values are not assigned to methods reliably in the flattened figure text, so no figure-only number is assigned.
rows.check: The values can be read from Figure 6 if its bars are in descending order. That order is consistent with the constant 21.0 control and 11.8 fine-tune values across Figure 14 and with the 'nearly double' ASR claim. On that reading, MLP offensive is about 41.0±5.5% mean compliance versus 21.0±5.6% with no intervention. Linking to none is correct.
